title: The sky we’re missing
summary: How much of each country lies under skies that hide the Milky Way? Eight maps, one raw dataset, and a visibility question.
image_alt: Maps of eight selected European countries. Modeled skyglow obscures the Milky Way over 51.9% of Belgium’s mapped area and 2.9% of Switzerland’s.
question: Where does artificial light obscure the Milky Way—and how much of each country does that cover?
approach: I classified the World Atlas’s raw sky-brightness cells using its Milky Way visibility cutoff, clipped them to country boundaries, and weighted each cell by its geographic area. The denominator is mapped area throughout; no population data are used.
finding: In this eight-country selection, about half of Belgium’s mapped area lies above the cutoff, compared with about 3% of Switzerland’s. The maps show where those areas fall, rather than using decorative shapes to stand in for geography.
limits: These are historical modeled estimates from 2014 satellite inputs, published in 2016. The eight countries are a selected comparison, not a Europe-wide ranking. Observing conditions affect real visibility. Maps are resized independently; compare the percentages, not silhouette size.
method_note: Cutoff: artificial zenith brightness >0.688 mcd/m². Native-resolution cells are area-weighted on the WGS84 ellipsoid. European territories only; generalized Natural Earth boundaries. Boundary inclusion changes every result by less than 0.4 percentage points. Full cutoff sensitivity and geographic scope are in the reproducibility files.
